strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: how to combine the data efficiency and interpretability of generative verifiers with the performance of discriminative PRMs, answered with a simple recipe (lightweight fine-tuning of reasoning models on ~1K filtered synthetic verification CoTs).

Comprehensive evaluation across many scenarios: standalone verification on ProcessBench, best-of-N on MATH-500/AIME'24, verifier-guided beam search, out-of-domain tasks (GPQA-Physics, LiveCodeBench), plus ablations on data scaling, process- vs outcome-based filtering, and difficulty-stratified analysis.

The headline claim of data efficiency (8K process labels vs ~712K for discriminative PRMs, with better F1) is well supported by the training-data scaling experiments (Fig. 1 left, Section 5.1), and OOD gains (+8% GPQA, +4.5% LiveCodeBench) over DiscPRMs are shown under matched base models.

Useful empirical findings beyond the main method: systematic documentation of LLM-as-a-judge failure modes (overthinking, looping, invalid judgments, prompt sensitivity, Table 3), and the demonstration that process-level filtering beats outcome-based filtering even with 2x fewer examples (Fig. 10).

Honest limitations section discussing score miscalibration, 'step label interference', and compute overhead of generative verification; training details, prompts, and hyperparameters are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
Extremely lightweight training (1K examples, hours on a single A100) makes the contribution practical and easy to build upon; code, data, and models are promised for release.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: generative/verbalized reward models via next-token prediction and critique training already exist (Generative Verifiers, GenRM, CLoud, Prometheus, Self-Taught Evaluators); the contribution is largely the combination with long-CoT reasoning models plus careful data filtering, so the delta over prior work should be stated more sharply.

A potential confounder weakens the 'data efficiency' framing: ThinkPRM inherits most of its verification ability from base models (R1-Distill-Qwen) that were themselves trained with massive compute and distillation data, so the comparison against DiscPRMs trained from the same base on more labels reflects fine-tuning data efficiency, not overall supervision/compute efficiency. The paper does not fully account for the pretraining/distillation investment or for the training compute of the teacher model (QwQ-32B used to generate data).

Inference-time compute is not compared on equal footing in all experiments: ThinkPRM generates up to 8192 tokens per verification while DiscPRM requires a single forward pass per step, yet 'outperforms under the same token budget' comparisons are confined to subsets (200 OmniMath problems) and appendix figures.

Evaluation uses small subsets (100 of 500 MATH-500 problems, 86 GPQA-physics questions, 200 LiveCodeBench problems) without variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests, so some reported gaps (e.g., 4.5-8% OOD) are hard to assess for reliability; single-run results appear standard throughout.

Scoring mechanism is somewhat ad hoc: forcing decode 'Is the solution correct?' and using P(yes)/(P(yes)+P(no)) after an 8192-token CoT is acknowledged to produce overconfident, near-binary scores; the interaction between long CoT and this forced-decode score deserves more analysis, and the miscalibration limitation may matter for search applications.

Minor presentation issues: the abstract conflates 8K process labels with 1K synthetic chains inconsistently across sections; several typos and incomplete sentences (e.g., 'We the difficulty' in E.8, 'Without particularly found QwQ...'), and release URL is empty; QwQ-32B variant remains clearly worse after fine-tuning without a satisfactory explanation.

strengths: The core empirical claim is valuable and clearly demonstrated: fine-tuning long-CoT reasoning models on only ~1K filtered synthetic verification chains (≈8K process labels) yields verifiers that match or beat discriminative PRMs trained on ~712K labels, across best-of-N, beam search, and out-of-domain tasks (GPQA-Physics, LiveCodeBench).

The diagnostic analysis of LLM-as-a-judge failures (invalid judgments, overthinking, infinite looping, prompt sensitivity in Table 3 and Figs. 4, 15, 16) is informative and well-documented with concrete examples.
The ablations are relevant: process- vs. outcome-based filtering (Fig. 10), training-data scaling for both THINKPRM and DiscPRM (Fig. 1 left, Figs. 22-23), and difficulty-binned analysis (Fig. 12).
Training is genuinely lightweight (LoRA, 1.5-4.5 hours on a single A100), and the filtering pipeline relies only on step-level labels, not gold rationales, making it plausibly scalable.
The limitations section (Section 5.4) honestly discusses overconfidence/uncalibrated scores, step label interference, and compute overhead.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work: the recipe is essentially rejection-sampling fine-tuning (STaR-style) applied to off-the-shelf reasoning models, closely following GenRM (Zheng et al., 2024), Critique-out-Loud (Ankner et al., 2024), self-taught evaluators (Wang et al., 2024), and generative verifiers (Zhang et al., 2024a). The main delta is using long-CoT base models and filtering with process labels, which is an incremental combination rather than a new method or insight.

The headline 'two orders of magnitude fewer labels' comparison is not fully compute- or protocol-matched. THINKPRM verification consumes thousands of tokens per solution (Figs. 2, 4), while DiscPRM is a single forward pass; the paper's own Section 5.4 concedes this overhead, yet the abstract and intro emphasize only label efficiency. The sequential-scaling comparison (Fig. 2) is run on only 200 problems, and parallel-vs-sequential results (Fig. 21) show no clear winner, weakening the 'scales verification compute' selling point.

Statistical rigor is thin: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; key results are on small subsets (100 MATH-500 problems, 86 GPQA-physics questions, 200 LiveCodeBench problems, AIME'24 with ~30 problems). Differences of a few points on such subsets (e.g., 4.5% on LiveCodeBench) may not be meaningful, yet they support strong claims in the abstract.

The synthetic data is distilled from QwQ-32B-Preview, so gains may largely reflect teacher capability plus format regularization rather than a general recipe; the QwQ-32B variant of THINKPRM itself performs notably worse (73.1/73.2 F1 in Table 2 vs. 87.3/85.7 for the 14B distill) and still has 7.9-15.1% invalid judgments, which the paper does not adequately explain or resolve.

Baseline fairness concerns: DiscPRM hyperparameters and score aggregation choices (last-step score, '+'/'-' tokens) are described only briefly; off-the-shelf PRM baselines differ in size and training data, making the 'surpasses off-the-shelf PRMs' comparison hard to interpret.

Potential train/test overlap: training data comes from PRM800K (built on MATH) while a main evaluation is MATH-500; the paper does not discuss contamination between the 869 unique training questions and the MATH-500 subset.

Presentation quality is below bar for a main-track submission: several grammatical errors ('Without particularly found QwQ to be hard to train', 'We the difficulty We do not estimate the difficulty', 'subtantial', 'high ha variance'), an empty release URL in footnote 1, and results spread across many figures that are hard to compare directly.

OOD generality is narrower than claimed: GPQA-physics and LiveCodeBench solutions are still step-structured mathematical/algorithmic reasoning in the same format the model was trained to verify; no genuinely different domains (e.g., open-ended text, non-step-structured tasks) are tested.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated research question: the paper identifies a genuine gap between data-efficient but weak LLM-as-a-judge verification and strong but supervision-hungry discriminative PRMs, and proposes a simple, sensible recipe (lightweight LoRA finetuning of long-CoT reasoning models on filtered synthetic verification chains).

Impressive data-efficiency results with a fair comparison design: THINKPRM matches or beats DiscPRM trained on the same base model using ~712K process labels while using only ~8K labels (1K chains), and additionally outperforms off-the-shelf PRMs (RLHFFlow-Deepseek-PRM, Math-Shepherd) despite being much smaller and trained on far less data.

Comprehensive and well-structured evaluation: multiple model scales (1.5B–32B), multiple generators, in-domain (MATH-500, AIME'24) and out-of-domain (GPQA-Physics, LiveCodeBench) settings, best-of-N and guided beam search, and both parallel and sequential verifier-compute scaling — the conclusions are not tied to a single model family or scaling mode.

Useful diagnostic analysis in Section 3.1 (invalid judgments, overthinking/infinite looping, prompt sensitivity of LLM-as-a-judge) with supporting histograms and appendix examples; these observations independently justify the approach and are valuable to practitioners.

Thoughtful ablations: process-based vs. outcome-based filtering (Fig. 10), training-data scaling (500→1K→65K chains, Figs. 22–23), difficulty-binned analysis (Fig. 12), and parallel vs. sequential scaling comparison under matched token budgets.

Honest limitations discussion (Section 5.4): score overconfidence/clustering, step label interference, and compute overhead of generative verification are acknowledged candidly, and the QwQ-32B variant's residual invalid-judgment rate is reported rather than hidden.

Good reproducibility: prompts (Figs. 13–14, 26), data statistics (Table 1), full training hyperparameters, and evaluation details (Appendix E) are provided; code, data, and models are promised for release.
weaknesses: Evaluation on small subsets limits statistical strength: only 100 MATH-500 problems and 86 GPQA-Physics questions, and headline OOD gains (8%, 4.5%) come from single points on these small sets; no confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or variance estimates are reported, so some claims (e.g., 'outperforms DiscPRM by 8%') rest on noisy measurements.
No significance testing or repeated-run analysis for the finetuning results; LoRA finetuning on 1K examples can exhibit run-to-run variance that is not characterized.

The data pipeline still fundamentally relies on gold process labels from PRM800K for filtering (all step decisions must exactly match gold labels); the 'data-efficiency' framing is fair, but the method's applicability in truly label-scarce regimes (silver Monte Carlo labels is only sketched, not evaluated).

The core recipe is an increment over prior generative-verifier work (GenRM, CoLM, critique-out-loud, self-taught evaluators); the main novelty is applying it to long-CoT reasoning models and demonstrating verifier-compute scaling, so originality is moderate even though the empirical contribution is solid.

Some presentation sloppiness: garbled sentences in Appendix C.1 ('Without particularly found QwQ to be hard to train') and E.8 ('We the difficulty We do not estimate...'), typos ('subtantial', 'syntehtic'), and the release URL footnote is empty; several results referenced in text (Table 2, Fig. 20-21) are relegated to appendices, slightly weakening the main-text narrative.

The sequential-scaling result (Fig. 2) is computed on only 200 OmniMath problems and relies on hand-picked trigger phrases whose effect the authors themselves admit may matter; conclusions about scaling behavior would benefit from broader evaluation.
The OOD claim of 'strong generalization' is somewhat overextended: the strongest 65K-trained model shows performance drops on OOD tasks (Appendix E.7), and only two OOD domains are tested.

strengths: Timely and practically significant question: reducing the supervision burden (hundreds of thousands of step labels) required to train process reward models, which is a real bottleneck for test-time scaling with PRMs.

Simple, well-motivated method: repurposing long-CoT reasoning models as generative PRMs via rejection-sampled synthetic verification chains, filtered only against step-level labels (not gold rationales), trained with lightweight LoRA/full fine-tuning. The pipeline is clearly described and appears reproducible (data generation prompt, filtering criteria, training hyperparameters in App. C).

Comprehensive and well-controlled evaluation: comparisons to a discriminative PRM built on the same base model (R1-Distill-Qwen) and trained on ~100x more process labels, plus LLM-as-a-Judge with the same base model, off-the-shelf PRMs (Math-Shepherd, RLHFFlow), and majority voting; results span ProcessBench, MATH-500, AIME'24, and OOD tasks (GPQA-Physics, LiveCodeBench), across best-of-N, beam search, and parallel/sequential verifier scaling.

Valuable analyses beyond headline claims: training-data scaling (Figs. 1/21/22), compute-matched comparison to self-consistency (Fig. 11), automatic Monte Carlo labels (Table 3), process- vs outcome-based filtering ablation (Fig. 9), generalization to long un-delimited reasoning traces (§5.2), difficulty-stratified gains (Fig. 23), and a candid limitations section (overconfidence/miscalibration, step label interference, inference overhead).

The diagnosis of LLM-as-a-Judge failure modes (invalid judgments, overthinking, infinite looping; Figs. 4, 5, 14) is a useful empirical contribution in its own right, with concrete evidence (length distributions, invalid-label rates).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a combination of known ingredients—generative verifiers/GenRM, rejection-sampling fine-tuning (STaR-style), and long-CoT distillation. The main contribution is the empirical demonstration and systematization rather than a new algorithm.

The 'data efficiency' claim partially conflates the method with the capability of modern long-CoT base models; while the base model is controlled across ThinkPRM/DiscPRM, the paper does not fully disentangle how much of the gain comes from the strong reasoning prior vs. the training recipe (e.g., no comparison of generative fine-tuning vs. same base with other objectives at equal label budget beyond the scaling study).

Evaluation on small subsets (100 MATH-500 problems, 86 GPQA-Physics questions, 200 LiveCodeBench problems) with no error bars, seed variance, or statistical significance testing; several claimed gaps (e.g., 4.5% OOD) rest on these small samples.

Contamination is not discussed: the base reasoning models (R1-Distill, QwQ) are trained on large web-scale math corpora, and evaluation benchmarks (ProcessBench subsets, MATH-500) may overlap with their training data, which could favor the generative verifier's pretraining priors.

Verifier inference cost is not rigorously accounted for against discriminative PRMs: ThinkPRM generates 1-8K verification tokens per step-scoring call, and the FLOPs-matched analysis is only against majority voting, not against DiscPRM-based selection at matched compute.

Writing quality issues throughout (e.g., 'uses uses', 'coreepond', 'We the difficulty', garbled sentence in C.1 about QwQ training, inconsistent Prompt/Single-label naming between Table 2 and Table 4), and the QwQ-32B finetuned model retains a high invalid-judgment rate (15.1%), weakening the claim that finetuning 'mostly fixes' these issues across all models.
No explicit statement of code/data release, which limits reproducibility of the data-generation pipeline despite detailed hyperparameters.

strengths: The central idea—finetuning open-weight long-CoT reasoning models into generative, verbalized PRMs using rejection-sampled synthetic verification chains filtered against PRM800K step labels—is simple, well-motivated, and clearly distinguishes the work from both discriminative PRMs and short-CoT generative verifiers (GenRM) and LLM-as-a-judge.

The evaluation is unusually broad: standalone verification F1 on ProcessBench subsets, best-of-N and guided beam search on MATH-500 and AIME '24, out-of-domain tests on GPQA-Physics and LiveCodeBench, long-CoT verification with Qwen3-1.7B, compute-matched comparison to self-consistency, and both parallel (@K) and sequential (budget-forcing) verifier scaling.

The analysis of LLM-as-a-judge failure modes (invalid judgments, overthinking, infinite looping; Figs. 4, 5, 14, 15; Table 4) is informative and directly motivates the finetuning approach, and the ablations are relevant: process- vs. outcome-based filtering (§5.6), training with automatic Monte Carlo labels (§5.4, Table 3), and training-data scaling up to 65K chains (§5.1, App. E.7).

Training is genuinely lightweight (1K chains, LoRA or full finetune in under 5 hours on a single A100), and the data pipeline relies only on step labels, not gold verification rationales, which the authors argue makes it scalable; the Monte Carlo-label experiment supports that claim.
The limitations section (§5.7) is honest and identifies real issues (score overconfidence at extremes, step label interference, inference overhead) rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is thin: several headline experiments use small test sets (100-problem MATH-500 subset, 200-problem OmniMath subset for sequential scaling, 86 GPQA-Physics problems) with no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests, even though differences between ThinkPRM and DiscPRM are sometimes a few points (e.g., Figs. 7, 8, 10).

Potential leakage/confound in the data-efficiency claim: training data comes from PRM800K (MATH-based), and MATH-500/AIME evaluations are effectively in-domain; the '100x fewer labels' comparison is also against a DiscPRM the authors trained themselves (App. C.2), whose hyperparameters (1 epoch, no warmup for the 14B) may be suboptimal, weakening the head-to-head claim, though comparisons to off-the-shelf PRMs (Fig. 8) partially mitigate this.

Verifier compute accounting is incomplete: ThinkPRM generates ~1K-8K token verification chains per solution, so best-of-N and beam-search comparisons against DiscPRM are not compute-matched; the compute-matched analysis (§5.3) is only against majority voting, not against discriminative verifiers.
Some baselines are not size-matched (e.g., ThinkPRM-1.5B vs. RLHFFlow-8B-Deepseek and Math-Shepherd-7B in Fig. 8), and long-CoT generalization (§5.2) is tested with only one small generator.

The manuscript has notable presentation defects: typos and broken sentences ('training uses uses synthetic data', 'coreepond', 'Without particularly found QwQ to be hard to train', 'We the difficulty We do not estimate the difficulty'), and inconsistencies (Table 2 random baselines vs. the 'random' line in Fig. 6; OmniMath invalid-rate for QwQ reported as 10.9% in §3 text area vs. 3.2% in Table 4), which undermine confidence in carefulness.

Originality is moderate: the approach is a combination of known techniques (rejection-sampling finetuning, generative verifiers, budget forcing), and the main contribution is the empirical demonstration that this recipe works well for process supervision rather than a new method or new theoretical understanding.

strengths: The central idea is compelling and clearly motivated: repurposing long CoT reasoning models as generative, verbalized PRMs, trained via rejection-sampled synthetic verification chains filtered only against step-level labels. This directly addresses the well-known data-efficiency bottleneck of discriminative PRMs.

The data-efficiency claim is well supported. Fig. 1 (left) shows ThinkPRM-14B trained on ~8K process labels outperforming DiscPRM-14B trained on the full PRM800K (712K labels), a two-orders-of-magnitude gap, with scaling curves over 500/1K/65K training chains.

Evaluation is broad and covers the scenarios practitioners actually care about: standalone verification (ProcessBench OlympiadBench/OmniMath), best-of-N (MATH-500, AIME '24), verifier-guided beam search, OOD transfer (GPQA-physics, LiveCodeBench), and compute-matched comparisons against self-consistency.

The verifier-compute scaling analysis (parallel @K sampling vs. sequential 'let's verify again' budget forcing, Fig. 2 and Fig. 20) is a genuine and interesting contribution unique to generative verifiers, and the parallel-vs-sequential comparison is a useful empirical finding.

Good ablations: process- vs. outcome-based filtering (Fig. 9), manual vs. Monte Carlo step labels (Table 3), prompt sensitivity of LLM-as-a-judge (Table 4), training-data scaling (Figs. 21-22), and per-difficulty analysis (Fig. 23).

The paper is refreshingly transparent: the limitations section (§5.7) honestly discusses overconfidence, 'step label interference', and inference overhead, and failure modes of the baselines are illustrated with concrete examples (Figs. 14-17).

Reproducibility is adequate: sampling/filtering criteria, prompts (Figs. 13, 26), LoRA/training hyperparameters (App. C), and dataset statistics (Table 1) are all specified; training costs are modest (hours on a single A100).
weaknesses: Evaluation subsets are small in several key experiments: only 100 of 500 MATH-500 problems, 30 AIME '24 problems, and 86 GPQA-physics questions. No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported anywhere, which is concerning for the smaller-margin comparisons (e.g., the 4.5% LiveCodeBench gain, differences between @4 and @8 scaling).

There is a teacher-capacity confound in the central comparison: ThinkPRM's synthetic data comes from QwQ-32B-Preview, a far stronger teacher than the R1-Distill base models used for both ThinkPRM and DiscPRM. The headline '1% of the labels' framing partly attributes to generative-vs-discriminative training what may stem from distilling a stronger model; a DiscPRM distilled from QwQ (or a generative PRM trained without the stronger teacher) would disentangle this.

Verifier overhead is under-quantified: the compute-matched FLOPs analysis (§5.3) compares against majority voting on solution FLOPs, but the F1/accuracy-vs-FLOPs comparison against the discriminative PRM under equal total compute (generator + verifier) is not systematically presented, despite §5.7 acknowledging the extra cost.

Internal inconsistencies and typos undermine confidence in polish: e.g., 'uses uses', 'coreepond', 'We the difficulty We do not estimate' (§E.9), QwQ's invalid-judgment rate differs between Fig. 5/Table 2 (7.9%) and Table 4 (18.3%), and QwQ-based ThinkPRM still has a high 15.1% invalid rate, which is acknowledged only in passing.

The claimed sequential-scaling advantage over LLM-as-a-judge (Fig. 2) is evaluated on only 200 OmniMath problems, and parallel scaling plateaus by K=4, so the 'scales verification compute effectively' claim has limited supporting range.
OOD robustness claims rest on two relatively narrow tasks (one physics MCQ subset, one code subset) and would benefit from broader domain coverage or repetition across seeds.
